fascĭcŭlus, i, m.dim.
fascis
,

la:noun:fas.gloss: dictates of religion, divine law (opp. iūs, human law), or an obligation thereunder
senses: dictates of religion, divine law (opp. iūs, human law), or an obligation thereunder
divine will or right, the will of God or heaven; a predetermined destiny
right, proper, allowable, lawful, fit, permitted, permissible, possible
la:noun:fas.html:
fas, indecl.n.
root fa-, cf. for; Gr. φημί, φά-ναι
Orig. belonging to the relig. lang., the dictates of religion, divine law; opp. to jus, or human law (rare; cf. also: aequitas, justitia): jus ac fas omne delere,; cf.: festis quaedam exercere diebus Fas et jura sinunt,: contra fas, contra auspicia, contra omnes divinas atque humanas religiones,.—Personified: audi Juppiter, audite Fines, audiat Fas,: prima deum Fas quae Themis est Graiis,: Fas omne mundi,i. e. the gods,.—
Transf.
A court-day, i. q. fastus (ante-class.): dies qui vocatur sic: QVANDO REX COMITIAVIT, FAS,, §§ 31, 32.—
In gen. (justice, equity, but usu. to be translated as an adjective), right, proper, allowable, lawful, fit, permitted; hence, possible (the predominant meaning of the word in prose and poetry; esp. freq. in the phrase fas est, with a subjectclause): fas, justum, pium, aequum subjici possunt honestati,: cum fas atque nefas exiguo fine libidinum Discernunt avidi,; ; cf.: quippe ubi fas versum atque nefas,; : jusque fasque est,: si jus, si fas est,: sicut fas jusque est,: ut eum nihil delectaret, quod aut per naturam fas esset aut per leges liceret,; cf.: quoad fas esset, quoad liceret,; and: huic legi nec obrogari fas est, neque derogari ex hac aliquid licet,: si me fas est orare etiam abs te, pater, etc.,: quid non adeptus est, quod homini fas esset optare?: si eos hoc nomine appellari fas est,: non esse fas, Germanos superare, si, etc.,: neque fas esse existimant, ea litteris mandare,: ad quos (libellos) interim respicere fas sit,: velut si aliter facere fas non sit,; ; ; 12, 7, 1: nec scire fas est omnia,: fas omne est, Cytherea, meis te fidere regnis,there is every reason,: si hoc fas est dictu,: neque id me facere fas existimo,: fas habere,; ; ; : leporem et gallinam et anserem gustare fas non putant,; fin.: fas prohibet, etc.,: contra quam fas erat,: ridetque (deus), si mortalis ultra Fas trepidat,: fas omne abrumpit,every right, obligation,: exuere,: et foedera respicere,; cf.: hostium quoque jus et sacra legationis et fas gentium rupistis,the law of nations,; so in Tac. freq. = jus: patriae,the right, claim of one's native land,: armorum,: disciplinae,

la:adj:fastus.html:
fastus, a, um, adj.
perh. root ΦΑ, φάσκω, φημί, fari; lit., in which it is allowed to speak
, fasti dies; and more commonly
absol.: fasti, ōrum, m. (acc. to the 4th decl. acc. fastus, Varr. ap. P.; ; ; ; Bentley (dub.); abl. fastibus, ), a publicists' t. t., a day on which judgment could be pronounced. on which courts could be held, a court-day (opp. nefasti, v. nefastus; cf. also: feriae, justitium, otium).
Prop.: ille (dies) nefastus erit, per quem tria verba (DO, DICO, ADDICO) silentur: Fastus erit, per quem lege licebit agi,; Müll. The register of these legal court-days, which for a long time existed only in the archives of the pontifices, was kept from the knowledge of the people, until Cn. Flavius, scribe to the Pontifex Maximus Appius Caecus, posted up a copy in the Forum: posset agi lege necne, pauci quondam sciebant, fastos enim volgo non habebant,; cf.: (Cn. Flavius) fastos circa forum in albo proposuit, ut, quando lege agi posset, sciretur,; ; .—
Transf.
In gen., an enumeration of all the days of the year, with their festivals, magistrates, events, etc., a calendar, almanac (syn.: annales, historia, res gestae, narratio, fabula): fastorum libri appellantur, in quibus totius anni fit descriptio: fasti enim dies festi sunt, Paul. ex Mull. N. cr.: ordo ipse annalium mediocriter nos retinet quasi enumeratione fastorum,: cum diem festum ludorum de fastis suis sustulissent,: fastos correxit (Caesar),: ut omne tempus ... ita in fastos referretur,; cf. .—
Esp.
The Fasti consulares, or registers of the higher magistrates, according to their years of service (v. Orelli, Onomast. Tullian. P. III.): quae (tempora) semel Notis condita fastis Inclusit volucris dies (i. e. fastis consularibus),: per titulos memoresque fastos,; so, memores,: tempora si fastosque velis evolvere mundi,: qui redit in fastos et virtutem aestimat annis, etc.,: in codicillorum fastis,: paginas in annalibus magistratuum fastisque percurrere,: ex fastis evellere,: hos consules fasti ulli ferre possunt,.—
Fasti Praenestini a Verrio Flacco ordinati et marmoreo parieti incisi, ; cf. , and the authors there cited; v. also Anthon's Dict. of Antiq. p. 432 sq.—
Fasti, the title of a poem of Ovid, on the Roman festivals, the festival-calendar; which, however, he completed for but six months of the year.

la:noun:fastus#2.gloss: A day on which courts sat
senses: A day on which courts sat
la:noun:fastus#2.html:
fastus, ūs (
gen. fasti, Coripp. 4, 137), m.
Sanscr. dharshati, to be bold; Gr. θρασύς, θάρσος; full form farstus
, scornful contempt or disdain of others, haughtiness, arrogance, pride (poet., and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: fastidium, clatio, superbia, arrogantia, insolentia).
Sing.: tu cave nostra tuo contemnas carmina fastu,; cf.: fastus inest pulchris sequiturque superbia formam,: superbo simul ac procaci fastu,: aspice primum, Quanto cum fastu, quanto molimine circum Spectemus,: tanto te in fastu negas, amice,i. e. thou withdrawest thyself with so much pride from my society,: fastus erga patrias epulas,—
Plur.: fastus superbi, ; .

la:noun:fascis.gloss: A faggot, fascine; bundle, packet, package, parcel.
senses: A faggot, fascine; bundle, packet, package, parcel.
A bundle carried by lictors before the highest magistrates, consisting of rods and an axe, with which criminals were scourged and beheaded.
A high office, like the consulship.
la:noun:fascis.html:
fascis, is, m.
cf. φάκελος, fascia, but v fido
,
a bundle of wood, twigs, straw, reeds, etc.
A fagot, fascine; a packet, parcel.
In gen. (rare): fasces stramentorum ac virgultorum,: lignorum,: magno comites in fasce libelli,: tot crimina, tot reos uno velut fasce complecti,.—Trop., of a crowd of people, .—
A burden, load: Romanus in armis Injusto sub fasce viam cum carpit,i. e. soldiers' baggage,; cf. Spald.: (apes) saepe ultro animam sub fasce dedēre,under the burden,: ego hoc te fasce levabo,: venales humero fasces portare,.—
In partic., in plur. fasces, a bundle carried before the highest magistrates, and consisting of rods and an axe, with which

criminals were scourged and beheaded.

Prop.: lictores duo, duo viminei fasces virgarum,: ut sibi (Tullo Hostilio) duodecim lictores cum fascibus anteire liceret, etc.,: anteibant lictores cum fascibus duobus,: fasces praetoribus praeferuntur,: Publicola statim secures de fascibus demi jussit,: tum demissi populo fasces, lowered (as a mark of respect) before the people, ; cf.: P. Valerius fasces primus demitti jussit,; for which: (P. Valerius) summissis fascibus in contionem escendit,; cf. under B.: paulo ante dimissi fasces,surrendered,: praecedebant incompta signa, versi fasces, at the funeral of Germanicus,: neque in litteris, neque in fascibus insignia laureae praetulit,; cf.: visus C. Marius cum fascibus laureatis,; so, laureati,: imperatorii,.—
Meton., a high office, esp. the consulship (poet.): qui petere a populo fasces saevasque secures Imbibit,: illum non populi fasces, non purpura regum Flexit,: ut si Detulerit fasces indigno, detrahet idem,; : et titulis et fascibus olim Major habebatur donandi gloria,; .—Of royalty: diadema Quirini Et fasces meruit,.—*
Trop., to give place, to acknowledge one's inferiority: cum tibi aetas nostra jam cederet fascesque summitteret,.

senses: extreme part, extremity of a thing
la:noun:fastigium.html:
fastīgĭum, ii, n.
cf. Sanscr. bhrshtīs, corner, rim; Gr. ἄ-φλαστον, aplustria, the ornamented stern of a ship; O. H. Germ. brort, the prow
,
the top of a gable, a gable end, pediment (syn.: cacumen, culmen, vertex, apex).
Prop.: Capitolii fastigium illud et ceterarum aedium non venustas, sed necessitas ipsa fabricata est ... utilitatem templi fastigii dignitas consecuta est,; cf.: fastigia aliquot templorum a culminibus abrupta,: evado ad summi fastigia culminis,; .—Hence, meton., the roof of a house, ; ; : habere pulvinar, simulacrum, fastigium, flaminem,; cf. of the same: omnes unum in principem congesti honores: circa templa imagines ... suggestus in curia, fastigium in domo, mensis in caelo,: Romae signa eorum sunt in Palatina aede Apollinis in fastigio,; cf. ; .—Transf.: operi tamquam fastigium imponere,.—
Transf.
The extreme part, extremity of a thing, whether above or below.
Top, height, summit: colles ... pari altitudinis fastigio oppidum cingebant,: opus nondum aquae fastigium aequabat,: summi operis,: jamque agger aequaverat summae fastigia terrae,: aquatilium ova rotunda, reliqua fere fastigio acuminata,: gracilitas (arundinis) nodis distincta leni fastigio tenuatur in cacumina,; cf.: cornua in leve fastigium exacuta,; ; .—In plur., : muri,: fontis fastigium,i. e. the height on which the fountain sprang up,.—
The lower part, depth: forsitan et scrobibus quae sint fastigia, quaeres,

what should be the depth of the trenches, .—

(From the sloping form of the gable.) A slope, declivity, descent: ab oppido declivis locus tenui fastigio vergebat,: jugum paulo leniore fastigio,: iniquum loci ad declivitatem fastigium,: rupes leniore submissa fastigio,: capreoli molli fastigio,; : musculi,: scrobes paulatim angustiore ad infimum fastigio,i. e. gradually narrowing from top to bottom,; cf.: si (fossa) fastigium habet, ut (aqua) exeat e fundo,.—
In the later grammarians, an accent placed over a word, ; ; P.
Trop.
The highest part, summit, the highest degree, most exalted rank or dignity (perh. only since the Aug. per.): quicquid numinum hanc Romani imperii molem in amplissimum terrarum orbis fastigium extulit,; cf.: sic fit, ut dei summum inter homines fastigium servent,: et quoad usque ad memoriam nostram tribuniciis consularibusque certatum viribus est, dictaturae semper altius fastigium fuit,; cf.: in consulare fastigium vehi,: ad regium fastigium evehere aliquem,: alii cives ejusdem fastigii,: stare in fastigio eloquentiae,: rhetoricen in tam sublime fastigium sine arte venisse,: et poësis ab Homero et Vergilio tantum fastigium accepit, et eloquentia a Demosthene,; cf.: magice in tantum fastigii adolevit, ut, etc.,grew into such esteem,.—
In gen., dignity, rank, condition: (M. Laetorio) curatio altior fastigio suo data est,; cf.: ampliora etiam humano fastigio decerni sibi passus est,: tamquam mortale fastigium egressus,: animus super humanum fastigium elatus,: quales ex humili magna ad fastigia rerum extollit Fortuna,.—
A leading or chief point, head in a discourse; a principal sort or kind (rare): summa sequar fastigia rerum,: e quibus tribus fastigiis (agrorum) simplicibus,sorts, kinds,: propter haec tria fastigia formae discrimina quaedam fiunt sationum,: haec atque hujuscemodi tria fastigia agri, etc.,; cf. also: quo fastigio sit fundus,fin. (and v. Lachm. ad ): laudem relego fastigia summa,.

la:noun:fastus.gloss: arrogance, pride, haughtiness; scornful contempt or disdain of others
senses: arrogance, pride, haughtiness; scornful contempt or disdain of others
la:noun:fastus.html:
fastus, ūs (
gen. fasti, Coripp. 4, 137), m.
Sanscr. dharshati, to be bold; Gr. θρασύς, θάρσος; full form farstus
, scornful contempt or disdain of others, haughtiness, arrogance, pride (poet., and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: fastidium, clatio, superbia, arrogantia, insolentia).
Sing.: tu cave nostra tuo contemnas carmina fastu,; cf.: fastus inest pulchris sequiturque superbia formam,: superbo simul ac procaci fastu,: aspice primum, Quanto cum fastu, quanto molimine circum Spectemus,: tanto te in fastu negas, amice,i. e. thou withdrawest thyself with so much pride from my society,: fastus erga patrias epulas,—
Plur.: fastus superbi, ; .

la:noun:fastidium.html:
fastīdĭum, ĭi, n.
cf. 2. fastus
,
a loathing, aversion for any thing, esp. for any sort of enjoyment (very freq. and class.; cf. taedium, nausea, etc.).
Lit., nausea, squeamishness, loathing, distaste for food: cibi satietas et fastidium,: mel fastidium creat,: fastidium abigere,: auferre,: discutere,: detrahere,.—In plur.: magna movet stomacho fastidia, etc.,; ; ; ; —
Esp. of a spoiled, pampered taste, niceness, daintiness, delicacy, : tantum in illis esse fastidium; ut nollent attingere nisi eodem die captum piscem,; cf. .—
Transf. to sight: oculorum in hominum insolentium indignitate fastidium,.—
Trop., dislike, aversion, disgust, fastidiousness.
In gen.: ab aliqua re celerrime fastidio quodam et satietate abalienari,; cf.: si (eloquentia) et ex copia satietatem et ex amplitudine fastidium tulerit, : nescis quantum interdum afferat hominibus fastidii, quantum satietatis,: satiari fastidio similitudinis,: nulla voluptas est, quae non assiduitate fastidium pariat,: vitato assiduitatis fastidio,: rudem esse omnino in nostris poëtis, aut inertissimae segnitiae est, aut fastidii delicatissimi,: quae habent ad res certas vitiosam offensionem atque fastidium,: audiendi,: insolens domesticarum rerum,: omnis stultitia laborat fastidio sui,: nec id fit fastidio meo,: ne sit fastidio Graecos sequi,: ipsum lignum in fastidio est,is despised,; cf.: aliquid fastidio damnare,: non omnia (i. e. arbores) in omnibus locis nasci docuimus, nec translata vivere: hoc alias fastidio evenit, fastidious or delicate nature, .—In plur.: non tam ea, quae recta essent, probari, quam quae prava sunt, fastidiis adhaerescere,; cf.: spectatoris fastidia ferre superbi,: opem ferre poëtis antiquis contra fastidia nostra,: matri longa decem tulerunt fastidia menses,.—
In partic. (with the notion of fastus predominating), scornful contempt, haughtiness, pride (syn.: elatio, vanitas, arrogantia, superbia, fastus): ex eorum (divitiorum) fastidio et superbia (regna) nata esse commemorant, Mos. N. cr.; cf.: superbiam magno opere, fastidium arrogantiamque fugiamus,; ; cf.: superbia et fastidio amplissimos honores repudiare,: si essent arrogantes, non possem ferre fastidium,: efferri fastidio et contumaciā,.—In plur.: superba pati fastidia?: oderunt fastidia divi,: qui tulerit Meroes fastidia longa superbae,: veteris fastidia quercus,.

la:verb:fastidio.html:
fastīdĭo, īvi, or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n. and a.
[fastidium], to feel disgust, loathing, or nausea, to shrink or flinch from any thing unpleasant to the taste, smell, hearing, etc.; to loathe, dislike, despise (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; cf.: taedet, reprobo, reicio, respuo, repudio).
Lit.
Neutr.: bi bendum hercle hoc est, ne nega: quid hic fastidis?; cf.: fastidientis stomachi est multa degustare,: majus infundam tibi Fastidienti poculum,: ut fastidis!.—
Act. (perh. not till the Aug. per.): num esuriens fastidis omnia praeter Pavonem rhombumque?: olus,: pulmentarium,: cactos in cibis,: fluvialem lupum,: vinum, Poët. ap. : euphorbiae sucus fastidiendum odorem habet,disgusting,: aures ... redundantia ac nimia fastidiunt,.—
Trop., of mental aversion, to be disdainful, scornful, haughty; to disdain, despise, scorn.
Neutr.: ut fastidit gloriosus!: vide ut fastidit simia!: in recte factis saepe fastidiunt,.—
With gen. (like taedet): fastidit mei,; so, mei, Titin. ap. : bonorum,.—
Act. (perh. not before the Aug. per.).
With acc.: (populus) nisi quae terris semota suisque Temporibus defuncta videt, fastidit et odit,: vilice silvarum et agelli, Quem tu fastidis,: lacus et rivos apertos,: vitium amici,: preces alicujus,: hoc lucrum,: grammatices elementa tamquam parva,: minores,: omnes duces post Alexandrum,: dominationibus aliis fastiditus (i. e. a prioribus principibus despectus),: ut quae dicendo refutare non possumus, quasi fastidiendo calcemus,: oluscula,.— Of inanim. or abstr. subjects: te cum fastidierit popina dives, etc.,: somnus agrestium Lenis virorum non humiles domos Fastidit umbrosamve ripam, .—In the part. perf.: laudatus abunde, Non fastiditus si tibi, lector, ero,; cf.: aliquem non fastiditis annumerare viris,: vetulus bos, ab ingrato jam fastiditus aratro,.—In the neutr. absol.: res ardua vetustis novitatem dare ... fastiditis gratiam, etc., praef. § 15.—In the part. fut. pass. with supine: quia (verba) dictu fastidienda sunt,.—
With an object-clause: a me fastidit amari,: jocorum legere fastidis genus,; : fastidit praestare hanc inferioribus curam,: fastidit balsamum alibi nasci,: an creditis, aequo animo iis servire, quorum reges esse fastidiant? et saep.: ne fastidieris nos in sacerdotum numerum accipere,: plebs coepit fastidire, munus vulgatum a civibus isse in socios,; .—Hence,
Adv.: fastīdĭenter, disdainfully, scornfully: parentibus fastidienter appellatis,.—
Part.: fastīdītus, a, um, in act. signif., disdaining, despising (post-Aug.): ne me putes studia fastiditum,.
la:verb:fastidio.inflection: īvi, or ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n. and a.

senses: a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck as a preventive against witchcraft
la:noun:fascinum.html:
fascĭnum, i, n. (-ĭnus, i, m.) [quasi bascanum, βάσκανον, Cloat. Ver. ap. ; but cf. Paul. ex ].
A bewitching, witchcraft, ; .—
Transf.
I. q. membrum virile (because an image of it was hung round the necks of children as a preventive against witchcraft; cf. Müll.), ; ; .—Also in the form fascinus, i. m., ; and personified, Fascĭnus, i, as a deity, the Phallus, .—
A kind of sea-shell, .

la:verb:fascino.gloss: to enchant, bewitch, charm, fascinate (especially by the eyes or tongue)
senses: to enchant, bewitch, charm, fascinate (especially by the eyes or tongue)
la:verb:fascino.html:
fascĭno, āre, v. a.
cf. Gr. βάσκανος, βασκαίνω, v. fascinum
,
to enchant, bewitch, charm, fascinate by the eyes or the tongue: nescio quis teneros oculus mihi fascinat agnos,: malā linguā,: contra fascinantes,: animal fascinatum,: vos non obedire veritati,.

la:noun:fascia.html:
fascĭa (fa/scea), ae, f.
kindred with fascis
,
a band, bandage, swathe, girth, fillet.
Prop. (to bind up diseased parts of the body; to wrap round the feet to prevent the boots from rubbing them; to bind under the breasts of women; a headband set with pearls, etc.; syn.: redimiculum, vitta, infula, diadema): devinctus erat fasciis,; ; ; ; cf.: fasciis crura vestiuntur,: cum vincirentur pedes fasciis, ap. ; (cf. with ); ; (with pedules); : carnem praependentem fascia substringere,: brachio lanis fasciisque obvoluto,: inflatum circa fascia pectus eat,; : vides illum Scythiae regem, insigni capitis decorum? si vis illum aestimare, fasciam solve: multum mali sub illa latet,; so of a diadem, : puero fasciis opus est, cunis, incunabulis,i. e. swaddling-cloths,: somniasse se, ovum pendere ex fascia lecti sui cubicularis,a bed-girth,; ; : uvas sole siccatas junci fasciis involvit,bands of rushes, mats,: nitor, qualem Bruttia praestabat calidi tibi fascia visci, plaster, .— Prov.: non es nostrae fasciae, i. e. of our rank or condition, .—
Transf. *
The casing of a door, Varr. ap. ; and 86, 10.—*
In archit., a wreath round a pillar, a listel, —*
A streak of cloud in the sky: nil color hic caeli, nil fascia nigra minatur,.—*
A zone of the earth: orbi terrae in quinque zonas, sive melius fascias dico, discernitur,, §§ 602, 607.

la:adj:fastidiosus.html:
fastīdĭōsus, a, um, adj.
fastidium
,
full of disgust or aversion.
Pass., that feels disgust, squeamish, disdainful, scornful, fastidious (class.).
Lit.: vaccae fastidiosae fiunt,: aurium sensus fastidiosissimus,: quod ille fastidiosus est,. —
Trop.: quamvis fastidiosus aedilis est,: in superiores contumax, in aequos et pares fastidiosus, in inferiores crudelis, etc.,: ex hac infinita licentia haec summa cogitur, ut ita fastidiosae, mollesque mentes evadant civium, ut, etc.,: Antonius facilis in causis recipiendis erat, fastidiosior Crassus,.— With gen.: C. Memmius perfectus Iitteris, sed Graecis: fastidiosus sane Latinarum,: dominus terrae Fastidiosus,: aestimator,i. e. that rates altogether too high,: fastidiosissimum mancipium,i. e. excessively haughty, proud,: est res difficilis, ardua, fastidiosa,.—
Act., that creates disgust, disgusting, loathsome, disagreeable (very rare; not in Cic.): fastidiosam desere copiam,: fastidiosā tristis aegrimoniā,. —Hence, fastīdĭōse, adv., squeamishly, scornfully, disdainfully, fastidiously (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. very rare): huic ego jam stomachans fastidiose, Immo ex Sicilia, inquam,: spectare,; cf.: diligenter et prope fastidiose judicare,: lente ac fastidiose probare,: recipior in coetum,: venditare aliquid,.—Comp.: fastidiosius ad hoc genus sermonis accedere,.

la:verb:fascio.html:
fascĭo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a.
fascia
, to envelop with bands, to swathe (post-Aug. and very rare): fasciato trunco,; .—Pass., .

senses: to slope up or down, to a point
la:verb:fastigo.html:
fastīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
v. fastigium
,
to make pointed, to sharpen to a point, to raise or bring to a point (in the verb. finit. only post-Aug., not in Cic.).
Lit.: frumenta verno tempore fastigantur in stipulam,grow up into a straw with a sharpened point,: folia in exilitatem fastigantur,: (terra) spatiosa modice paulatim se ipsa fastigat,: se molliter (Africa),; .—In the part. perf.: scutis super capita densatis, stantibus primis, secundis summissioribus ... fastigatam, sicut tecta aedificiorum sunt, testudinem faciebant,: collis in modum metae in acutum cacumen a fundo satis lato fastigatus,: fastigatus in mucronem,: fastigatā longitudine (margaritarum),.—
Transf.
(Cf. fastigium, I. B. 2.) Fastigatus, sloping up to a point, sloped; sloping down, steep, descending: collis leniter fastigatus paulatim ad planitiem redibat,: tigna ... prona ac fastigata, ut secundum naturam fluminis procumberent,.—
(Cf. I. B. 3.) In the later grammarians, to mark with an accent, to accent: ut fastigetur, longa brevisve fuat,.—
Trop., to elevate, exalt (late Lat.): qui statum celsitudinis tuae titulorum parilitate fastigat,: quamquam diademate crinem Fastigatus eas,.—Hence, fastīgātus, a, um, P. a., high, exalted (late Lat.): ad arcem fastigatissimae felicitatis evectus,. 4: duo fastigatissimi consulares,.—Adv.: fastīgāte, ; .
